```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE, out.width = "100%")
set.seed(20261029)

jack_se <- function(t_loo) {
  n <- length(t_loo)
  sqrt((n - 1) / n * sum((t_loo - mean(t_loo))^2))
}
mdeq <- read.csv("../../data/flint_mdeq.csv")
x <- mdeq$lead
n <- length(x)
med_loo <- sapply(1:n, function(i) median(x[-i]))

vt <- read.csv("../../data/flint_vt.csv")
lx <- log(vt$first_draw)
ly <- log(vt$flush_2min)
n_vt <- nrow(vt)
B <- 4000
r <- cor(lx, ly)
r_loo <- sapply(1:n_vt, function(i) cor(lx[-i], ly[-i]))
se_r <- jack_se(r_loo)
boot_cor <- replicate(B, {
  i <- sample(n_vt, replace = TRUE)
  cor(lx[i], ly[i])
})
boot_w <- replicate(B, {
  i <- sample(n_vt, replace = TRUE)
  a <- lx[i]
  b <- ly[i]
  (cor(a, b) - r) / jack_se(sapply(1:n_vt, function(j) cor(a[-j], b[-j])))
})
pct <- quantile(boot_cor, c(0.025, 0.975), names = FALSE)
bt <- r - se_r * quantile(boot_w, c(0.975, 0.025), names = FALSE)
ci <- function(v) sprintf("[%.3f, %.3f]", v[1], v[2])

flint <- data.frame(lx, ly)
loo_mse <- function(d) {
  fit <- lm(ly ~ poly(lx, d), data = flint)
  mean((resid(fit) / (1 - hatvalues(fit)))^2)
}
train_mse <- function(d) mean(resid(lm(ly ~ poly(lx, d), data = flint))^2)
```

## The jackknife SE

$T_{(i)}$ is the statistic computed without $x_i$, using `x[-i]`.

$$\widehat{\text{SE}}_{\text{jack}}(T) = \sqrt{\frac{n - 1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n \left(T_{(i)} - \bar T_{(\cdot)}\right)^2}, \qquad \bar T_{(\cdot)} = \frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n T_{(i)}.$$

- For the mean, the sample variance of the $T_{(i)}$ is only $s^2 / (n - 1)^2$. The factor $(n - 1)/n$ makes the SE exactly $s / \sqrt n$.
- $n$ evaluations and no Monte Carlo error. The bootstrap takes $B$ evaluations.
- Flint, correlation of logged first draw and flushed: jackknife SE `r sprintf("%.4f", se_r)`, bootstrap SE `r sprintf("%.4f", sd(boot_cor))`.

## Failure case: the median

- The leave-one-out medians take two values, $x_{(m)}$ and $x_{(m+1)}$ for $n = 2m$, or three for odd $n$.
- So the jackknife SE depends only on the gap between the two middle observations.
- MDEQ: `r sum(x == median(x))` of `r n` samples equal the median, so every $T_{(i)}$ is `r median(x)` ppb and the jackknife SE is `r jack_se(med_loo)`.
- For normal data the ratio of jackknife to true SE tends to an Exponential(1), not to 1.
- The jackknife needs a smooth $T$: a mean, variance, correlation or regression coefficient. For quantiles, bootstrap.

## The bootstrap-$t$ interval

Studentize each bootstrap replicate with an SE from **its own** bootstrap sample:
$$W^*_b = \frac{T^*_b - T}{\widehat{\text{SE}}^*_b}, \qquad \left[T - \widehat{\text{SE}} \, W^*_{1 - \alpha/2}, \; T - \widehat{\text{SE}} \, W^*_{\alpha/2}\right].$$

- A nested bootstrap costs $B \times B_2$ evaluations. A jackknife in each sample costs $B \times n$.

| Flint correlation, $r =$ `r sprintf("%.3f", r)` | 95% interval |
|---|:-:|
| percentile | `r ci(pct)` |
| bootstrap-$t$ | `r ci(bt)` |

- The SE of a correlation shrinks as it grows, so the bootstrap-$t$ reaches further down.

## Cross-validation

- **Training error** scores $\hat f$ on the points that chose it, so it is optimistic.
- **Leave-one-out**: average $L(Y_i, \hat f_{(i)}(X_i))$. For least squares, one fit gives every $e_i / (1 - h_{ii})$.
- **$K$-fold**: fit to $K - 1$ random folds, predict the one left out. Use the same folds for every model.

| Flint, `poly(lx, d)` | $d = 1$ | $d = 5$ | $d = 10$ |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| training MSE | `r sprintf("%.3f", train_mse(1))` | `r sprintf("%.3f", train_mse(5))` | `r sprintf("%.3f", train_mse(10))` |
| leave-one-out MSE | `r sprintf("%.3f", loo_mse(1))` | `r sprintf("%.3f", loo_mse(5))` | `r sprintf("%.3f", loo_mse(10))` |

## Choosing a loss

With $e = y - \hat y$, a constant prediction $c$ that minimizes each loss is

| loss | $L(e)$ | best $c$ |
|---|:-:|:-:|
| squared | $e^2$ | mean |
| absolute | $\lvert e \rvert$ | median |
| pinball | $\tau e$ if $e > 0$, $(1 - \tau)(-e)$ if $e \le 0$ | $\tau$ quantile |

- With $\tau = 0.9$, predicting one unit too low costs 9 times as much as one unit too high.
- Write down what each kind of error costs, and use that loss. Cross-validation works with any loss.
